summary: Ordinals put 第 dì before the number: 第一 ‘first’, 第二 ‘second’ … 第十 ‘tenth’, 第十一, 第一百 — no number is irregular, and 一 keeps its first tone (dì-yī). Before a noun the measure word follows: 第三个孩子 ‘the third child’, 第二本书 ‘the second book’; nouns that count themselves take none: 第一天 ‘the first day’, 第二年 ‘the following year’. ‘Which one (in order)?’ is 第几: 他是第几个？. Many numbered things use the bare number as their ordinal, without 第: months (三月 ‘March’), weekdays (星期三 ‘Wednesday’), dates (五月一号 ‘1 May’), floors (三楼), centuries (二十一世纪) and decades (八十年代 ‘the eighties’). ‘Last’ is 最后 (最后一天 ‘the last day’); ‘half’ is 一半 on its own (我吃了一半) and 半 before a measure word or after the hour (半个小时, 三点半); a quarter of an hour is 一刻: 三点一刻 3:15, 三点三刻 3:45. Dates and times run from big to small: 2026年十月九号星期五上午十点一刻.

blocks.title: The measure word comes after
blocks.text: 第 + number + measure word + noun: 第三个孩子, 第二本书. Nouns that count themselves need none: 第一天, 第二年, 第五课 ‘lesson five’.

blocks.title: Half and quarter
blocks.text: 半 is half PAST the hour: 三点半 = 3:30. There is no *两刻: half an hour is 半个小时. 一刻 and 三刻 are the only quarters; 一刻钟 is a quarter of an hour as a length (我等了一刻钟).

blocks.caption: Big to small: year, month, day, weekday, part of the day, time

blocks.title: Years are read digit by digit
blocks.text: 一九九五年 yī jiǔ jiǔ wǔ nián, 二〇二六年 èr líng èr liù nián — not ‘nineteen ninety-five’. In writing years are mostly digits: 1995年.

items.title: 半 — bound
points: 半个小时 half an hour

items.title: 一半 — free
points: 我吃了一半。 I ate half.
一半的学生是女孩。 Half of the students are girls.

blocks.title: 一 keeps its tone
blocks.text: In ordinals, dates and numbers read digit by digit, 一 stays yī: 第一 dì-yī, 一月 yīyuè, 一号 yī hào, 一九九五年 yī jiǔ jiǔ wǔ nián. Before a measure word or 百 / 千 it changes as usual: 一个 yí ge, 一天 yì tiān, 第一百 dì-yìbǎi.

blocks.title: 最后 — the last
blocks.text: 最后 + number + measure word: 最后一个 ‘the last one’, 最后一天 ‘the last day’. ‘Last’ meaning ‘previous’ is 上: 上个星期 ‘last week’. As an adverb 最后 is ‘finally, in the end’ (C19).

blocks.title: Asking
blocks.text: 他是第几个？ ‘what number is he (in the line)?’ · 今天几月几号？ ‘what’s the date today?’ · 现在几点？ ‘what time is it?’ · 你的生日是几月几号？

askYourself: Is it a rank or a place in a series (the third child, the first day)? → 第 + number (+ measure word).
Does the noun count itself (天, 年, 课)? → no measure word: 第一天.
Is it a month, a weekday, a date, a floor, a century or a decade? → the bare number, no 第.
Is it ‘last’? → 最后 (final) or 上 (previous).
Is it half? → 半 before a measure word or after the hour; 一半 on its own.
Is it a quarter of an hour? → 一刻 (15), 三刻 (45) — never *两刻.
Is it a date or a time? → big to small: year, month, day, weekday, time.
steps: Choose: 第 + number, or the bare number.
Add the measure word if the noun needs one.
Order dates and times from big to small.

traps: *第两 → 第二 (ordinals always use 二).
*第三月 for ‘March’ → 三月; 第三个月 is ‘the third month (of a stay)’.
三楼 is ‘the third floor’; ‘three storeys’ is 三层.
*两刻 → 半 (三点半, 半个小时).
*第二十一世纪 → 二十一世纪.
*最后个月 for ‘last month’ → 上个月.

quiz.why: Ordinals use 二, and the measure word follows the ordinal.
Months are named with the bare number; 三个月 is ‘three months’.
一刻 is a quarter of an hour; the hour comes first.
半 is half past; there is no 两刻.
Centuries take the bare number; 二十一个世纪 would be ‘twenty-one centuries’.
最后 + number + noun; 上 means ‘previous’.
In ordinals 一 keeps its first tone.
Big to small: the month, then the day.

notes.text: Greek ordinals are adjectives that agree (πρώτος, πρώτη, πρώτο), and dates use cardinals except the first (πρώτη Μαΐου but δύο Μαΐου); Chinese ordinals never agree, and dates use plain numbers throughout: 五月一号, 五月二号.
Russian ordinals agree like adjectives (первый, первая), and dates use the ordinal (первое мая); Chinese dates use the plain number (五月一号) and 第 never changes.
Spanish ordinals agree (primero / primera) and dates use cardinals except, often, the first (el uno / primero de mayo); Chinese 第 + number never changes.
English has irregular ordinals (first, second, third) and writes dates small-to-big or month-first; Chinese ordinals are all regular (第 + number) and dates go big → small: 2026年十月九号.
French says le premier but then cardinals for dates (le deux mai) — like Chinese 五月二号 with a plain number; French ordinals -ième are regular after premier, Chinese ones all regular with 第.

German ordinals take adjective endings (der erste, am dritten Tag) and dates use them (am ersten Mai); German writes the date small → big (1. Mai 2026), Chinese big → small (2026年五月一号), with plain numbers.
Hindi has irregular first ordinals (पहला, दूसरा, तीसरा, चौथा), then -वाँ (पाँचवाँ), agreeing in gender; Chinese has 第 + number for all.
Persian adds -om to the number (dovvom ‘second’, sevvom ‘third’) — one suffix for all, close to Chinese 第 + number; ‘first’ is avval or yekom.
Arabic ordinals are adjectives of the pattern فَاعِل that agree in gender (الثَّالِثُ / الثَّالِثَةُ ‘the third’), with أَوَّل ‘first’; Chinese 第三 never changes.
Hebrew ordinals agree in gender (רִאשׁוֹן / רִאשׁוֹנָה) and exist only up to ten; above ten the cardinal is used. Chinese builds every ordinal with 第.
Turkish has one ordinal suffix -(i)nci with vowel harmony (birinci, ikinci, üçüncü) — one rule for all numbers, as Chinese has one prefix 第.
Japanese uses the same 第 (第一 だいいち) as well as 〜番目 (二番目 ‘the second’); dates and years also go big → small: 2026年10月9日.
Korean uses Sino-Korean 제 (제일 ‘first’, from 第一) and native 첫째, 둘째, 셋째; dates go big → small, like Chinese.
Finnish ordinals are words of their own (ensimmäinen, toinen, kolmas …) and take case endings; Chinese ordinals are 第 + the unchanged number.
Hungarian adds -dik (harmadik ‘third’, negyedik ‘fourth’) after első, második; like Chinese, dates run big → small (2026. október 9.).
Swahili forms ordinals with -a + number (kitabu cha tatu ‘the third book’), with kwanza ‘first’ and pili ‘second’; Chinese uses 第 + number + measure word: 第三本书.
Vietnamese thứ + number (thứ ba ‘third’, thứ nhất ‘first’) works like 第; its weekdays are numbered too (thứ hai ‘Monday’), as 星期一 is.
Words in polysynthetic languages are built from many suffixes; Chinese ordinals are the opposite extreme — one separate prefix, 第, before an unchanged number, the same for every number.

seeAlso.note: der erste, zweite, dritte … -te / -ste with adjective endings; dates with ordinals (am ersten Mai), written small → big (1. Mai 2026); Chinese: 第 + number, dates big → small with plain numbers (2026年五月一号).
Arabic ordinals are adjectives that agree in gender (الْيَوْمُ الثَّالِثُ / السَّنَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ); Chinese 第三天, 第三年 — 第 never changes.
Hebrew ordinals agree in gender (רִאשׁוֹן / רִאשׁוֹנָה) up to ten, then cardinals; Chinese builds every ordinal with 第.
The clock (点, 分, 半) and the date (年, 月, 号) were introduced in S15; here they are completed with 刻 and the ordinals.
